title: Sriram Balaji Is India's Last Man Standing at Wimbledon. The Chennai Doubles Specialist Is Making the Most of It.
excerpt: After a breakthrough quarter-final at Roland Garros last month, India's top-ranked doubles player has carried that momentum to the All England Club with an assured first-round start alongside Brazilian partner Marcelo Demoliner.
body:
There are no Indian names in the singles draws at Wimbledon this year. No Nagal. No Bhambri. No long-shot qualifier to root for on Court 18 while pretending to work. For a country of 1.4 billion people, the absence is conspicuous.

But on Court 8, in the gentlemen's doubles, there is Sriram Balaji.

The 36-year-old from Chennai and his Brazilian partner Marcelo Demoliner made a confident start to their Wimbledon 2026 campaign on Wednesday, clinching the opening set 6-3 against the Belgian-Dutch pairing of Sander Gillé and Sem Verbeek. The Indo-Brazilian combination controlled play from the baseline, used aggressive net approaches, and converted half their break points while winning a remarkable 84 per cent of points behind their first serve.

It was the kind of performance that has defined Balaji's quietly excellent 2026 season — and the latest chapter in an improbable late-career surge that has turned India's most overlooked tennis player into its most successful.

## The Roland Garros Breakthrough

A month ago, Balaji and Demoliner reached the quarter-finals at Roland Garros — Balaji's maiden Grand Slam quarter-final in any discipline. They beat the sixth-seeded German pair of Kevin Krawietz and Tim Pütz in straight sets to get there, an upset that made headlines in Chennai but barely registered elsewhere.

That run ended against the second seeds, Harri Heliövaara and Henry Patten, but it established something important: the Balaji-Demoliner partnership is not a one-tournament curiosity. It is a functioning, competitive Grand Slam doubles team.

Earlier in the year, the duo won Challenger titles in Pau and Nonthaburi, building the kind of match-by-match rhythm that doubles partnerships need. Balaji is currently ranked World No. 74 in ATP doubles — a career best — and is firmly India's top-ranked male doubles player.

## What Makes the Partnership Work

Doubles is a specialist's game, and Balaji has the right profile for it. He is a disciplined server (his first-serve percentage in the Wimbledon opener was 67 per cent), a sharp volleyer, and a smart court reader who compensates for what he lacks in raw power with positioning and anticipation.

Demoliner, at 37, brings the physicality. At 6-foot-4, the Brazilian is an imposing presence at the net, and his reach on volleys gives opponents fewer passing angles. The two have developed a natural understanding of each other's movement patterns — who covers the centre, who takes the wide ball, how to rotate on returns.

It is the kind of chemistry that only regular tournament play together can produce, and it is paying dividends at the moments that matter.

## India's Doubles Tradition

Balaji's rise comes at an awkward moment for Indian tennis. Rohan Bopanna, who carried the flag for Indian doubles for two decades, retired from the professional tour in 2025 after a career that included a Grand Slam title (2024 Australian Open, with Matthew Ebden) and an ATP Masters 1000 crown at Indian Wells.

Bopanna's departure left a gap that Balaji has filled more convincingly than anyone anticipated. While Yuki Bhambri and Saketh Myneni remain in the picture for Davis Cup, it is Balaji who has been consistently present on the biggest stages this year.

India has a richer doubles heritage than its singles record might suggest. The names stretch back decades: Leander Paes, Mahesh Bhupathi, Sania Mirza. Balaji does not have their name recognition, but he is, at this moment, producing the most consistent men's doubles Grand Slam results that India has seen since Bopanna's peak.

## What Comes Next at Wimbledon

If Balaji and Demoliner close out their first-round match, they will face a tougher draw in the second round. But grass suits their game — the fast surface rewards net play and clean volleying, both strengths of the partnership.

The All England Club is where doubles matches can take on a life of their own. The later rounds draw bigger crowds, the atmosphere shifts, and a hot partnership can ride momentum deep into the second week.

For the thousands of Indian-origin fans in London who will be streaming through the Wimbledon gates this fortnight, Balaji gives them someone to follow — and a reason to linger on the outer courts. The Centre Court may belong to Sinner and Djokovic. Court 8 belongs to Chennai.

## A Late-Career Bloom

At 36, Balaji is in the unusual position of playing the best tennis of his life. He has won more matches, earned more ranking points, and performed better at Slams in 2026 than in any previous season. It is the kind of late bloom that doubles, with its lower physical toll and premium on experience, occasionally allows.

He will not be on any billboards. He will not trend on social media. But he will be on court at Wimbledon, doing what very few Indian tennis players are doing right now: winning.

That should be enough.
